t: Minimum Cost to Acquire Required Items
o: Buy b bundle items (each covers one unit of both requirements) plus singles to cover the remainder; overshooting is allowed. Cost as a function of b is f(b) = b*costBoth + max(0, need1-b)*cost1 + max(0, need2-b)*cost2. Example 1: bundles are so cheap that buying 3 costs 3. Example 2: bundles are expensive, so b = 0 and the cost is 2*5 + 3*4 = 22. Example 3: nothing needed, cost 0. Since needs reach 1e9 we cannot try every b — but f is convex, so only a few candidate points matter.
k: f(b) is piecewise linear and convex: its slope costBoth - [b<need1]*cost1 - [b<need2]*cost2 is non-decreasing in b.
A convex function attains its minimum at a breakpoint; the only breakpoints are b = 0, b = min(need1, need2), b = max(need1, need2).

a.i: The slope of f changes only when b crosses need1 or need2 (indicators switch off). Hence f is linear between consecutive points of {0, min(need1,need2), max(need1,need2), ∞}, and its global minimum lies at one of the three finite breakpoints. Evaluate f there and take the best — O(1) regardless of need magnitudes.
s: Define f(b) as above (watch max(0, ...) for overshoot).
Let m = min(need1, need2), M = max(need1, need2).
a.t: O(1) — three evaluations of a closed-form function

a.i: Because f is convex over integers, ternary search on b in [0, min(need1,need2)]... note the domain must extend to max(need1,need2) since overshooting can help; searching [0, max(need1,need2)] with integer ternary search also finds the minimum in O(log) evaluations and is a safe fallback if you doubt the breakpoint analysis.
s: While hi - lo > 2, compare f(m1) and f(m2) at the two interior thirds and shrink.
Evaluate f on the remaining 2-3 integers and return the minimum.
a.t: O(log(max(need1, need2))) — ternary search halving the interval by thirds

w: The breakpoint method is the interview winner: derive convexity, name the three candidates, done. Pitfall: restricting b to at most min(need1, need2) — example 1 shows overshoot via bundles can be optimal. Use 64-bit products (needs up to 1e9 times costs up to 1e6). Follow-up: three requirement types, or limited bundle stock.
